title: Goldman Sachs Now Sees Fed Hiking Rates Again in October
excerpt: After calling an end to the Fed's tightening cycle, Goldman reverses course and forecasts a consecutive 25-basis-point increase — while the bank's own asset-management arm bets on a skip until December.
body:
Goldman Sachs now expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 25 basis points at its October policy meeting, adding a further hike to its September call and positioning itself as one of the first major Wall Street banks to forecast consecutive rate increases.

In a note to clients on Thursday, the bank said October was the most likely timing for the next move because it was most natural to deliver hikes that the Fed itself framed as supporting "a timelier return" to its 2% inflation target at back-to-back meetings. The call marks a reversal of Goldman's earlier view that the Fed had completed its tightening cycle with September's quarter-point increase — a sign of how Wednesday's meeting forced investors and economists to reassess the path of US rates.

Context & Background

The Fed on Wednesday raised its policy rate to a 3.75%-4.00% range, its first increase in three years, after months of pressure to hold steady from President Trump, who has publicly demanded cuts. The vote was unanimous, and the updated Summary of Economic Projections — the "dot plot" — showed a 16-2 majority of officials expecting at least one more hike this year, with four policymakers forecasting two additional increases.

Goldman said the meeting was more hawkish than expected, citing the rate projections, an upward revision to the neutral interest rate, and Chair Kevin Warsh's repeated description of the move as having only "removed a dose of accommodation." On inflation, the bank noted policymakers increasingly favored a quicker return to the 2% target — a posture it read as an endorsement of consecutive moves rather than a stop-start cycle.

There is one notable dissenting voice inside Goldman's own orbit. Kay Haigh, global head of fixed income at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, told Reuters the central bank will likely skip the October meeting because of its proximity to the midterm elections, and instead deliver one more hike in December. "The Fed has signaled it does not at this stage envisage an aggressive tightening cycle," she said. "Most FOMC members see a total of two hikes this year per the SEP."

Impact & Analysis

Markets are now pricing a far more hawkish path than they were a week ago. Traders on the CME FedWatch tool see roughly 50% odds of another quarter-point hike in October, up sharply after the Fed signaled further tightening could be needed. Odds of one more increase this year sat at nearly 52%, with the probability of a larger 50-basis-point move above 35%, according to Barron's.

Wall Street is lining up behind the tighter view. Bank of America Global Research — the only brokerage more aggressive than Goldman — is projecting hikes in both October and December. Morgan Stanley and Australia's Macquarie added a March 2027 hike to their existing December calls, reflecting a growing "higher-for-longer" consensus.

Goldman is also shifting its inflation diagnosis. Before the decision, its economists had argued the case for a hike was "weak," saying demand wasn't excessive and supply shocks from high oil and fuel prices would correct themselves once the war ended, according to CNN. The Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel refineries are the problem — "all of it," Goldman's economists said. Oil above $100 a barrel has since made that patience look harder to defend.

Not everyone agrees the tightening is wise. Michael Pearce, chief US economist at Oxford Economics, warned that rate hikes are ineffective against supply-driven inflation. "The economy is solid and can withstand a few rate hikes, but the risk is higher interest rates begin to weaken the labor market," he said.

"I don't believe that we need to do harm to the labor markets to achieve our objective."

— Kevin Warsh, Federal Reserve Chair

Diaspora Angle

For the Indian diaspora in the US, a second consecutive hike lands directly on mortgages, auto loans, and credit card debt at a moment when many first-generation households are buying homes or financing education. Higher US rates also strengthen the dollar, easing costs for families remitting money to India, while pressuring India's own central bank to weigh whether to defend the rupee — a tradeoff with real consequences for NRI deposit rates and bond yields.

What's Next

The October meeting is now the main event: Goldman's consecutive-hike call against the bank's own asset-management arm betting on a skip. Traders' 50% October odds will swing on the CPI prints between now and then, and on the path of energy prices. With the Bank of England deciding Thursday and the Bank of Japan on Friday, the global rate picture is tightening in step — a synchronized move the diaspora will feel on both sides of the Pacific.
